title: What it asks
hook: scholars list its conditions: knowledge, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission

segments.voice: Yesterday, becoming Muslim, and your line: said sincerely. Did you give the welcome you chose? Today, what the two sentences ask of the one who says them. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

A key with no teeth will slide into a lock and turn nothing. Imam al-Bukhari, at the head of a chapter in his collection, records a saying of an early teacher, Wahb ibn Munabbih. Someone asked him whether la ilaha illallah is the key to Paradise. Yes, he said. But every key has teeth. Bring a key with its teeth, and the door opens for you. Bring one without, and it won't. So what are the teeth? Later scholars tried to name them.

One list some scholars teach is called the conditions of la ilaha illallah. Not extra rules added on, but what it takes for the words to be more than sound. First, knowing. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "So know (O Muhammad) that there is no God save Allah." Know, not just repeat. Someone saying it should understand what the no and the yes mean, the way this week has tried to open them. Second, being sure. Certainty, yaqin. The Qur'an describes the true believers as those who believe in Allah and His messenger "and afterward doubt not." Some who teach this list draw a line here: a question passing through the mind isn't the same as doubt that has settled in. Asking, as this year began, is welcome. Third, sincerity. Saying it for God, not for a marriage, a job, or a crowd's approval. The Qur'an says people were commanded to serve Allah "keeping religion pure for Him." Pure there means unmixed, said for one audience. Then the rest of the list: truthfulness, so the tongue and the heart say the same thing; love, for God and for what the words point to; acceptance, taking the whole of the testimony and not just the comfortable part; and submission, letting it shape what you actually do. Notice what the list is for. Not to sit in judgment over someone else's shahadah. Yesterday's story ruled that out: no one splits open a heart. It's a mirror, held up by people who wanted to check their own key.

The practice: pick one condition to work on. Settle, and breathe. Let the list pass slowly through your mind: knowing, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission. Notice which one catches. Whether you're Muslim or not, you can ask the same of anything you say you stand for: do I know it, am I sure of it, do I mean it? Choose one, and stay with it for the rest of the sit, without grading yourself. If you pray, you can ask for help with that one. The bell holds the time.
What it asks. The conditions of the testimony: the teeth on the key, starting with knowing, being sure, and meaning it. Today's word.
Your line: knowing, sure, sincere. Today, before you say something you care about, check it against those three. Tomorrow, oneness, explained. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Muslim teachers explain the shahadah through its conditions, using the list as a way for believers to examine their own faith rather than to judge others'.

notes: Editor: the conditions list is presented as one list some scholars teach, not the scholars' list; 'much later' and 'scholars who teach this list are careful' softened (teach, myth, trapdoor).
Pickthall 47:19, 49:15 and 98:5 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording (especially 'afterward doubt not' and 'keeping religion pure for Him').
Wahb ibn Munabbih's 'key with teeth' saying is from al-Bukhari's chapter heading (tarjama) in the Book of Funerals, not a numbered hadith; confirm the placement and paraphrase.

The list of conditions follows the index (knowledge, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission). The script gives no count and calls it 'the list scholars teach'; some scholars add an eighth (rejecting what is worshiped besides God) or arrange it differently. 'Much later' is deliberately vague about when the list was formalized; Keeper may add who.
'Scholars who teach this list are careful here' about passing questions vs settled doubt: a general claim; Keeper to confirm.
The teach ties back to day 1067's Usama story ('no one splits open a heart').
